WeaveLA: Event Driven Cross-Subtask Latent Memory Weaving
for Repetition-Aware Robot Manipulation

Shoujing Zhu1,*,‡\ddagger  Zhenyang Liu1,3,*  Fungmiu Wong1,*  Jiafeng Wang1  Bo Yue2 Guiliang Liu2,4  Simo Wu1  Xiangyang Xue1,†\dagger  Taiping Zeng1,†\dagger 1 Fudan University  2 School of Data Science, The Chinese University of Hong Kong, Shenzhen  3 Shanghai Innovation Institute  4 Shenzhen Loop Area Institute {zhusj25, liuzy24, fmwang23, jfwang25}@m.fudan.edu.cn, boyue@link.cuhk.edu.cn, liuguiliang@cuhk.edu.cn, wusimo19911125@gmail.com
{xyxue, zengtaiping}@fudan.edu.cn * Equal contribution  ‡\ddagger Project Lead  †\dagger Corresponding author
Abstract

Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies have achieved remarkable single-step manipulation, yet they remain brittle precisely where each stage depends on what was just completed. The core issue is structural: short-window VLAs lack an explicit channel for rouxting information across sub-task boundaries, and existing memory-augmented variants either write at every frame, retrieve from demonstration-time stages, or fire at sub-goal events without performing an explicit sub-task-to-sub-task hand-off into the action expert. We identify the sub-goal completion event as the natural temporal unit for cross-subtask memory hand-off, and present WeaveLA (Weave Latent memory for Vision-Language-Action policies), a cross-subtask memory interface that, on top of a frozen VLA backbone, compresses each completed segment into latent tokens via query-driven attention pooling and routes them directly into the action-generation path of the next sub-task. This event-triggered, action-side design preserves the base policy’s short-window interface while adding a lightweight cross-subtask channel. Through stratified evaluation on RoboMME with a π0.5\pi_{0.5} backbone, WeaveLA’s gains land exactly where the channel is needed: on the hardest repetition slice (SwingXtimes, N=3N{=}3), success rises from 0%0\% to 47.8%47.8\%, while single-execution episodes remain unchanged. Per-episode paired analysis confirms the gains are confined to tasks whose causal structure requires cross-subtask information.

   

1 Introduction

Robotic manipulation has witnessed remarkable progress in recent years, largely propelled by the scaling of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies. Models such as RT-2 [5], OpenVLA [17], π0\pi_{0}/π0.5\pi_{0.5} [4, 29], and the GR00T N1.x family [25, 26] achieve impressive single-step manipulation by conditioning on the current observation [45], proprioceptive state, and natural-language instruction within a short temporal window. They reliably grasp objects, press buttons, and place items in compact contexts [28, 34].

However, a large fraction of real-world manipulation work is not single-step but repetitive: an assembly cell repeats the same insertion motion, a packaging station places NN items into a bin until full, a quality-control fixture stops the cube only after the right number of swings. The defining property of such episodes is not their length but their cross-subtask dependency — what to do at the current stage depends on what was just completed at the previous one. Current short-window VLAs collapse precisely here: not because they cannot execute the primitive, but because once one sub-task ends the next is launched without any compact summary of what just happened. There is no explicit channel for routing information across sub-task boundaries, and the policy has no persistent signal that the previous stage has been completed.

Recent memory-augmented VLAs attempt to address this by adding temporal context projection to the policy — through multi-frame summaries, visual-trace overlays, growing memory banks, or retrieval over demonstration-time stages. These methods differ in what they store and where they consume it, but they almost all share the same default when: write at every frame, over a sliding window, or via demonstration-stage retrieval. A more recent line [51, 7, 49, 50, 13] fires writes at sub-goal events but stops short of a true cross-subtask hand-off that matters for repetitive manipulation — none of these triggers delivers a self-contained summary to the next sub-task’s action expert. We provide a detailed comparison in Section 2.

We identify a key principle: the sub-goal completion event is the natural temporal unit at which cross-subtask information becomes available, and the next stage begins to depend on it. A per-frame writer must implicitly discover boundaries from dense observations and pays a per-step memory cost; a demo-stage retrieval mechanism cannot key onto rollout-time progress. Writing precisely at the sub-goal event aligns the information hand-off with the causal structure of repetitive tasks — the moment one stage ends is exactly when the next stage needs to know what was accomplished.

Based on this principle, we present WeaveLA, a cross-subtask latent memory weaving interface for repetition-aware robot control. At each sub-goal completion event, a Query-driven Memory Weaver uses 8 learnable query tokens [21] to compress the just-completed segment into a compact latent (N=8N{=}8 tokens, d=2048d{=}2048) via single-step attention pooling, and routes this latent directly into the action-generation path of the next sub-task — not the language prompt, not the visual context. The action-side injection ensures cross-subtask information reaches the motor-execution level without being diluted through the VLM backbone. We instantiate the interface on π0.5\pi_{0.5} via AdaRMS modulation of the Gemma action expert. The pretrained backbone remains frozen, and only a lightweight Weaver module and an action-side memory modulation are trained, preserving the base policy’s competence on non-repetitive tasks.

Through stratified evaluation on RoboMME, WeaveLA delivers gains that land exactly where the cross-subtask channel is needed. On the hardest repetition slice — SwingXtimes at N=3N{=}3, where the policy must keep track of how many back-and-forth motions have already happened — success rises from 0%0\% to 47.8%47.8\%. Critically, single-execution episodes (N=1N{=}1) remain at ∼100%\sim 100\% in both conditions, confirming that the mechanism activates only where the channel is required rather than acting as a generic capacity boost. Per-episode paired analysis on 800 matched episodes confirms the imbalance is confined to tasks whose causal structure demands cross-subtask information.

In summary, our contributions are:

  1. 1.

    We identify the sub-goal completion event as the natural temporal unit for cross-subtask memory hand-off, and argue the hand-off should deliver a self-contained summary of the just-completed sub-task directly to the next sub-task’s action expert — a when-axis design dimension under-explored by per-frame and demonstration-retrieval memory mechanisms.

  2. 2.

    We propose WeaveLA, a query-driven attention-pooling memory interface that writes 8 latent tokens at each sub-goal boundary and feeds them directly into the action-generation path. The pretrained VLA backbone is preserved untouched; only a small Weaver module and an action-side projection are trained.

  3. 3.

    Through repetition-stratified, difficulty-stratified, and per-episode paired analyses on RoboMME, we provide mechanism-aligned evidence: WeaveLA’s gains land where the cross-subtask channel is needed and stay quiet where it is not, with the strongest single result moving SwingXtimes N=3N{=}3 from 0%0\% to 47.8%47.8\%.

2 Related work

2.1 Memory-augmented VLA policies

Memory-augmented VLA policies differ along three axes: what is stored, where it is consumed, and when the write is triggered. Prior work stores dense visual histories or overlays [19, 43, 10, 44], semantic traces or retrieved episodes [36, 32, 22], and recurrent/query summaries [30, 20]; these memories are consumed through prompt/input augmentation [22, 16, 24], planner-level memory [32, 42], or action-path modulation. WeaveLA targets the last setting with a compact event-level latent routed directly into the next sub-task’s action expert.

Along the when axis — the write trigger — existing methods either write at every frame or retrieve from demonstration-time stages, and a more recent line [51, 7, 49, 50, 13], alongside a longer history of skill-segment IL [18, 53, 52], fires at sub-goal/segment events but never delivers a self-contained hand-off to the next sub-task’s action expert. WeaveLA identifies the sub-goal completion event as the natural write trigger and contributes on the hand-off side, routing a compressed per-segment latent directly into the action expert.

2.2 Query-bottleneck memory modules

Learnable query bottlenecks are a general mechanism for compressing variable-length context into a fixed-size latent set. They bridge frozen vision and language modules in BLIP-2’s Q-Former [21], support hierarchical or cross-segment context in robot and sequence models [42, 6], and appear in imitation-learning abstractions that compress variable-length sub-segments [18]. The trigger–weaver factorisation we adopt is directly inspired by MemGen [46], which couples a learned trigger with a learned latent weaver for text-LLM reasoning; WeaveLA retargets that factorisation to embodied control by replacing sentence boundaries with sub-goal completion events and routing the latent into the action-generation path of a frozen VLA. Thus the query bottleneck summarises a just-completed sub-task segment for a downstream action expert, rather than a single image for language generation. We compare single-step attention pooling with a Q-Former-style decoder stack and find that the simpler attention-pooling extractor is more stable in the rollout-time, action-grounded regime (Section 4.4).

2.3 Task-structure priors and repetition counting

Repetitive manipulation is not a niche academic problem: industrial work such as assembly, packaging, inspection, polishing, and kitting often requires executing the same primitive a prescribed number of times, where the hard part is knowing should next move is repetitive. Control-side task-structure methods make this state explicit through reward machines [37] or LTL-conditioned policies [38], which expose automaton states at sub-task boundaries. WeaveLA shares the view that boundaries are informationally privileged, but replaces hand-specified symbolic state with a learned latent shaped end-to-end by action prediction. Perception-side repetition work instead focuses on recognising or counting repeated activity in video [9, 15, 31, 27, 41]. These works address the perceptual question of recognising repetitions; WeaveLA addresses the complementary control question: once a sub-task has just been completed, how should that event be routed into the policy so the next stage is conditioned on it?

3 WeaveLA architecture

3.1 Overview

WeaveLA targets manipulation episodes that decompose into ordered sub-tasks ℰ=(τ0,τ1,…,τK−1)\mathcal{E}=(\tau_{0},\tau_{1},\ldots,\tau_{K-1}). A standard VLA policy predicts an action chunk [48, 39] ata_{t} from the current observation oto_{t}, proprioceptive state sts_{t}, and language instruction ℓ\ell. WeaveLA adds one cross-subtask memory channel: at the completion event of τk−1\tau_{k-1}, a compact latent mk−1m_{k-1} summarises the just-completed segment and conditions the action expert throughout τk\tau_{k}. The interface is action-side — the language prompt and visual context of the base policy are unchanged — and the pretrained backbone is frozen except for low-rank adapters and a small Weaver module. Figure 2 summarises the three architectural components: (A) a frozen perception backbone, (B) a query-driven Memory Weaver triggered at sub-goal completion events, and (C) action-side memory conditioning.

3.2 Sub-goal-event trigger

A central design choice distinguishes WeaveLA from per-frame [19] and demo-stage retrieval [22] memory: the memory write is triggered only at sub-goal completion events during rollout. For simulation experiments, sub-goal boundaries are provided by the simulator, isolating the memory mechanism from the boundary-detection problem. A sub-goal completion event eke_{k} is associated with segment τk−1\tau_{k-1} (frames between ek−1e_{k-1} and eke_{k}); between events, the action expert continues to be conditioned on the most recent mk−1m_{k-1}. Figure 1 illustrates the trigger schedule on a 3-block placement task.

The sub-goal event aligns the memory write with the natural unit at which the next stage depends on the previous one — the same temporal abstraction that the options framework [35, 2] formalises through option termination conditions. We deliberately do not assume the resulting latent encodes any particular structured quantity; whatever it encodes is shaped by the downstream action-prediction loss.

3.3 Query-driven memory weaver

For a completed segment τk−1\tau_{k-1}, we extract perceptual features from the segment’s frames: visual tokens projected from the frozen vision encoder of the underlying VLA, and projected proprioceptive state tokens. These are concatenated and layer-normalised [1] into a multimodal feature sequence H∈ℝB×L×dhH\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times L\times d_{h}}. A fixed set of N=8N{=}8 learnable query latents Q∈ℝN×dhQ\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d_{h}} summarises HH via a single attention-pooling step [40]:

A=softmax⁡(Q​K⊤dh),mk−1=Wout​(A​V+Q),A=\operatorname{softmax}\!\Bigl(\tfrac{QK^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_{h}}}\Bigr),\qquad m_{k-1}=W_{\text{out}}\,(A\,V+Q), (1)

where K=V=HK{=}V{=}H and WoutW_{\text{out}} is a learned linear projection to the memory width d=2048d{=}2048. We use dh=1024d_{h}{=}1024 for the latent space and d=2048d{=}2048 at the output. The query residual +Q+Q preserves a non-zero gradient path to the queries when the attention pattern is sharp. The memory is segment-local: each mk−1m_{k-1} is computed only from the perceptual features of τk−1\tau_{k-1}, and we do not feed mk−2m_{k-2} back into the encoder. This independent-per-hop design also matches what we found training-stable; see Section 3.5 and Appendix A.11 for the staged-training analysis.

3.4 Action-side memory consumption

π0.5\pi_{0.5} instantiation.

Each action-expert Gemma [11, 12] block in π0.5\pi_{0.5} [29] already contains two timestep-conditioned AdaRMS modules (one before self-attention, one before the FFN). WeaveLA leaves both untouched and inserts a third, memory-conditioned AdaRMS step between the self-attention residual and the existing pre-FFN AdaRMS, so the base time-conditioning pathway is preserved. Given Weaver tokens M∈ℝB×N×dmM\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times N\times d_{m}} with N=8N{=}8, we project them to the action-expert width, M~=M​Wm∈ℝB×N×dact\tilde{M}=MW_{m}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times N\times d_{\mathrm{act}}}. For action hidden states Xℓ∈ℝB×T×dactX_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times T\times d_{\mathrm{act}}} at layer ℓ\ell, the memory context (with RoPE [33] on QQ/KK and RMSNorm [47] pre-norm) is

Qℓ\displaystyle Q_{\ell} =RoPE⁡(RMSNorm⁡(Xℓ)​WℓQ),\displaystyle=\operatorname{RoPE}(\operatorname{RMSNorm}(X_{\ell})W_{\ell}^{Q}), (2)
Kℓ\displaystyle K_{\ell} =RoPE(RMSNorm(M~)WℓK),Vℓ=RMSNorm(M~)WℓV,\displaystyle=\operatorname{RoPE}(\operatorname{RMSNorm}(\tilde{M})W_{\ell}^{K}),\qquad V_{\ell}=\operatorname{RMSNorm}(\tilde{M})W_{\ell}^{V},
Cℓ\displaystyle C_{\ell} =ConcatHeads⁡[softmax⁡(Qℓ​Kℓ⊤dhead+ℳ)​Vℓ]​WℓO,\displaystyle=\operatorname{ConcatHeads}\!\left[\operatorname{softmax}\!\left(\tfrac{Q_{\ell}K_{\ell}^{\top}}{\sqrt{d_{\mathrm{head}}}}+\mathcal{M}\right)V_{\ell}\right]W_{\ell}^{O},

where ℳ\mathcal{M} masks padded memory slots. The token-wise context then produces scale and shift parameters for the memory-conditioned AdaRMS modulation,

[γℓ,βℓ]=Cℓ​WℓΔ+bℓΔ,Xℓ′=Xℓmean⁡(Xℓ2)+ε⊙(1+γℓ)+βℓ.[\gamma_{\ell},\beta_{\ell}]=C_{\ell}W_{\ell}^{\Delta}+b_{\ell}^{\Delta},\qquad X_{\ell}^{\prime}=\frac{X_{\ell}}{\sqrt{\operatorname{mean}(X_{\ell}^{2})+\varepsilon}}\odot(1+\gamma_{\ell})+\beta_{\ell}. (3)

This design keeps memory modulation lightweight: it only adjusts the AdaRMS scale/shift, masks invalid memory tokens, and starts near the unmodulated RMSNorm behaviour via near-zero initialisation.

3.5 Staged training strategy

Training proceeds in three stages, separating action grounding, memory warmup, and full integration. Stage 0 performs task-set adaptation with the vision encoder frozen and only the flow-matching action loss active — this establishes a competent short-window policy on the target task family before any memory mechanism is introduced. Stage 1 (K=2K{=}2 multi-subtask windows) introduces the Weaver and the memory-conditioning pathway, but trains them only against the action loss; this gives the memory pathway enough time to stabilise before semantic auxiliary objectives are added. Stage 2 (variable K∈{2,3,4}K\in\{2,3,4\}) enables the full objective with semantic alignment and contrastive auxiliaries.

We also tested a single merged stage that combines all three objectives from the beginning. Despite stable action and alignment loss curves, the raw memory latent norm decayed monotonically across training (a hidden representation collapse not visible in the loss curves), and downstream evaluation success collapsed to near-zero. Action-grounded warmup before semantic objectives is therefore not an arbitrary curriculum choice but a necessary stabilisation of the memory pathway. We provide the diagnostic weaver_latent_norm metric and the merged-stage failure curve in Appendix A.11 (Figure 7).

3.6 Training objective and computational footprint

Action loss.

The primary objective is the base policy’s flow-matching action loss [23]. Given a clean action chunk aa and a noise sample ϵ∼𝒩⁡(0,I)\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I), we sample t∼Beta⁡(1.5,1)t\sim\mathrm{Beta}(1.5,1) on (0,1](0,1] (diffusion-style convention: t=1t{=}1 is noise, t=0t{=}0 is the clean action) and form at=t​ϵ+(1−t)​aa_{t}=t\,\epsilon+(1-t)\,a. The action expert predicts the velocity field vθ(at,t∣ot,st,ℓ,mk−1)v_{\theta}(a_{t},t\mid o_{t},s_{t},\ell,m_{k-1}) conditioned on the observation, state, instruction, and Weaver memory mk−1m_{k-1}, and we minimise

ℒaction=𝔼t,a,ϵ∥vθ(at,t∣ot,st,ℓ,mk−1)−(ϵ−a)∥22.\mathcal{L}_{\text{action}}\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{t,a,\epsilon}\,\bigl\|v_{\theta}(a_{t},t\mid o_{t},s_{t},\ell,m_{k-1})-(\epsilon-a)\bigr\|_{2}^{2}. (4)

Sub-goal annotations are training-time supervision only.

In Stage 2 we additionally use a memory–text alignment loss ℒalign\mathcal{L}_{\text{align}} and a memory contrastive loss ℒctr\mathcal{L}_{\text{ctr}}, weighted at 0.050.05 and 0.020.02 respectively. The total loss is ℒ=ℒaction+λalign​ℒalign+λctr​ℒctr\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{action}}+\lambda_{\text{align}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{align}}+\lambda_{\text{ctr}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{ctr}}. Both auxiliaries operate on a tokenised description of the just-completed sub-goal — ℒalign\mathcal{L}_{\text{align}} matches the Weaver latent to a text encoder embedding of the sub-goal description, and ℒctr\mathcal{L}_{\text{ctr}} pulls together latent–text pairs from the same trajectory while pushing apart pairs from different trajectories. This sub-goal text is consumed only during training. At inference time the policy receives only the original episode-level instruction; sub-goal completion events drive the memory write, but no sub-goal text is fed to the model. The auxiliaries serve to shape the latent space during training; they do not change the model’s input interface at deployment.

Computational footprint.

Trainable parameters consist of three groups: (i) PaliGemma  [3] LoRA  [14] adapters in the π0.5\pi_{0.5} backbone, (ii) the Weaver query latents and projection matrices, and (iii) the action-side memory cross-attention and AdaRMS scale/shift projections. In total the trainable parameter count is approximately 4646M, on top of the frozen ∼3.4\sim 3.4B-parameterr base policy — about 1.4%1.4\% of the base model. Because the memory write is triggered only at sub-goal boundaries rather than every frame, the runtime cost of the memory channel during rollout is negligible compared to dense per-frame memory mechanisms; a per-frame writer with the same latent size would incur a memory-extraction forward pass at every observation step.

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental setup

Benchmark.

We evaluate on RoboMME [8], which reports per-task success rates over 50 episodes per task across 16 manipulation tasks split into Easy / Medium / Hard sub-pools. The two repetition tasks (PickXtimes, SwingXtimes) sample episodes whose natural-language instruction encodes a target count NN specifying the number of sub-goals to be executed in that episode (e.g., N=3N{=}3 means three pick-and-place repetitions before the stop button is pressed). Unless context indicates the memory bottleneck width (where N=8N{=}8 is fixed throughout, except in the width ablation of Appendix A.10), NN refers to this sub-goal count. Main-text figures report results on the six tasks used for π0.5\pi_{0.5} training; the full 16-task breakdown is in Appendix A.1.

Why SwingXtimes and StopCube are hard.

Both tasks share a defining property absent from non-repetitive RoboMME tasks: the correct action at the current stage cannot be inferred from the current observation alone. SwingXtimes [8] requires the policy to swing a cube back and forth NN times between two targets and then press a stop button. The instruction encodes NN, but visually the scene at swing 11 and swing 33 is indistinguishable — the cube and the targets occupy the same positions. The policy must carry a persistent signal of how many swings have already occurred. StopCube [8] requires the policy to remain static and press a stop button only after the cube has reached a target the prescribed number of times; here too the visual scene is ambiguous between the “not yet” and the “now” moments, and the decision to press is determined by the trajectory of the previous stages. Tasks like ButtonUnmask or PickHighlight, by contrast, can be solved by reactively responding to the current observation. The repetition / dependent-stop tasks are therefore a clean stress test for whether a policy can route information across sub-task boundaries; failures on these tasks isolate the cross-subtask channel as the bottleneck.

Backbones and instantiations.

The main results in Sections 4.2–4.3 use a π0.5\pi_{0.5} backbone with attention-pooling Weaver (denoted “π0.5\pi_{0.5}+AP”). For RoboMME we report two training scales: 6-task (PickXtimes, ButtonUnmask, ButtonUnmaskSwap, PickHighlight, StopCube, SwingXtimes) and 16-task (all RoboMME tasks); all four π0.5\pi_{0.5}+AP runs (Weaver-on/off ×\times 6-task/16-task) share training stages, differing only in the Weaver mechanism and the training-task set. We further probe two orthogonal axes of the design: an extractor study (single-step attention pooling vs. Q-Former-style multi-layer decoder, “π0.5\pi_{0.5}+QF”; Section 4.4) and a trigger-source study (oracle vs. model-internal latent-shift detector with the extractor fixed at attention pooling; Section 4.5). Full hyper-parameters are in Appendix A.12.

4.2 Aggregate results

Figure 3 reports per-task success on the six trained tasks for π0.5\pi_{0.5}+AP. The aggregate average improves from 19.0%19.0\% (Weaver off, 6-task) to 24.7%24.7\% (Weaver on, 6-task), with the largest improvements on SwingXtimes (32%→56%32\%\to 56\%) and StopCube (8%→22%8\%\to 22\%) — the two tasks identified above as requiring cross-subtask information. At the 16-task scale the same framework improves from 17.3%17.3\% to 23.3%23.3\%, again driven by the repetition / dependent-stop tasks. These aggregates are a starting point; the following analyses test whether the gains land where the cross-subtask channel is actually needed. The full per-task numerical table is in Appendix A.2.

4.3 Repetition-stratified analysis

The aggregate numbers understate where the mechanism actually engages. Figure 4 stratifies per-episode outcomes on the two repetition tasks by the instruction-encoded sub-goal count NN. With N=1N{=}1 (a single sub-goal, no cross-subtask dependency), both Weaver-on and Weaver-off succeed at ∼100%\sim 100\%, as expected: a single execution does not depend on a previously completed sub-goal. As soon as N≥2N{\geq}2, the gap opens, and it widens with NN.

The headline finding lives in the hardest sub-population. On SwingXtimes at N=3N{=}3 (three sub-goals required), Weaver-off succeeds in 0%0\% of episodes; Weaver-on succeeds in 47.8%47.8\%. The same setting at the 16-task training scale moves from 4%4\% to 30%30\%. This is the slice where the cross-subtask channel is most critical: the visual scene is ambiguous between an unfinished and a near-finished swing trajectory, and only a persistent signal from previously completed sub-goals can determine the correct action.

Pooling across both repetition tasks at the 6-task scale, Weaver-on succeeds on 24.6%24.6\% of N≥2N{\geq}2 episodes against 7.2%7.2\% for Weaver-off — a 3.4×3.4\times relative improvement. At the 16-task scale the same pool gives 17.4%17.4\% versus 5.8%5.8\% (3.0×3.0\times relative). The sign and shape are stable across data scales. The neutrality at N=1N{=}1 is as informative as the gap at N≥2N{\geq}2: a mechanism that improved N=1N{=}1 would betray that its gains came from incidental capacity rather than from the cross-subtask channel. The StopCube reference levels overlaid in Figure 4 show that the same mechanism-localisation pattern holds on the dependent-stop task as well, even though it does not have an explicit NN-stratification axis. The full NN-stratified table is in Appendix A.3.

Repetition stratification gives the cleanest view of where the mechanism engages, but two further analyses confirm the same pattern. Difficulty stratification on the six trained tasks shows the gain concentrates on Hard episodes (1.4%→12.5%1.4\%\to 12.5\%), while Easy and Medium episodes change only marginally. Per-episode paired analysis on the same matched 50 episodes per task confirms the localisation directly: counting episodes that only one condition solves, Weaver-on uniquely succeeds on 1313 episodes vs. 11 for Weaver-off on SwingXtimes, and 88 vs. 11 on StopCube; on every other task the two counts differ by at most 33. Both stratifications mirror the NN-stratified picture: the cross-subtask channel engages exactly on the tasks whose causal structure requires it. Full tables are in Appendix A.4 (difficulty) and Appendix A.5 (paired contingency).

StopCube as a what/where/when ablation.

StopCube is the canonical count, time-critical task in RoboMME [8]: the policy must press the button at the NN-th moment a moving cube reaches the target. We read StopCube as a one-axis-at-a-time ablation around our anchor WeaveLA at 22.0%\mathbf{22.0\%}; Figure 5 shows what each one-axis swap costs. Varying what is stored, every alternative collapses to single digits because the substituted representation cannot carry the per-event count signal: recurrent state (TTT, RMT) compresses count into a diffuse hidden state, sparse perceptual (TokenDrop+Modul) drops the slow continuous evidence, non-oracle symbolic (GroundSG+QwenVL) compounds subgoal-prediction errors across visits, and the rich-perceptual-but-count-blind prior baselines MemER [32] and SAM2Act+ [10] target keyframe retrieval / waypoint prediction rather than count tracking, figure 5 showing baseline numbers from Table 12 of Dai et al. [8]. Only a dense per-frame buffer (FrameSamp+Modul, 42.0%42.0\%) beats us. Varying where or when, neither axis explains that gap: within the FrameSamp family the where trend is monotone (visual context 13.7%→13.7\%\to separate expert 28.9%→28.9\%\to action-side AdaLN 42.0%42.0\%) and WeaveLA already sits at the peak’s where; along when, no-write and per-step append both fall below ours, per-keyframe retrieval underperforms because retrieved frames are not aligned with count events, and per-frame writes win only by paying a per-step cost. The residual gap therefore sits on the what axis (per-event count latent vs. dense per-frame buffer); the two strongest mechanisms share the same where (action-side modulation) and differ on what/when, suggesting FrameSamp’s dense buffer and WeaveLA’s per-event latent are orthogonal and could in principle be combined as parallel modulation streams (left to future work). Per-method numerical deltas and failure-mode analysis are in Appendix A.9.

4.4 Extractor design study: attention pooling vs. Q-Former

Replacing the single-step attention-pooling Weaver (Eq. 1) with a multi-layer decoder Q-Former [21] extractor (same trigger, same AdaRMS consumption, 16-task scale) collapses 16-task success from 23.3%23.3\% to 3.5%3.5\% (π0.5\pi_{0.5}+QF), with 56.3%56.3\% of episodes terminating by rollout timeout rather than wrong action — attributable to higher inference cost and a less stable training trajectory (full numbers in Appendix A.7). We adopt attention pooling throughout.

4.5 Trigger source robustness: mechanism is decoupled from oracle

To verify that the simulator-provided sub-goal boundaries used in Sections 4.2–4.3 are not a load-bearing oracle, we fix the WeaveLA extractor and replace the trigger with a model-internal alternative: the Stage 2 contrastive auxiliary ℒalign+ℒctr\mathcal{L}_{\text{align}}+\mathcal{L}_{\text{ctr}} shapes the Weaver latent to align with sub-goal text embeddings, and we re-purpose this representation as a deployment-time event detector by firing a memory write when the projected latent’s EMA cosine distance from the segment anchor exceeds a calibrated threshold (Appendix A.8). No external supervision is used at deployment.

The mechanism’s lift replicates without oracle.

The 16-task aggregate is indistinguishable (Table 1 left): latent-shift 17.4%17.4\% vs oracle 17.0%17.0\% vs no-memory 16.25%16.25\%. Crucially, the mechanism-localisation signature of Figure 4 replicates exactly under latent-shift on SwingXtimes: N=1N{=}1 saturates at 100%100\%, and on the hardest slice (N=3N{=}3) latent-shift rises from 4%4\% to 21.7%\mathbf{21.7\%}, recovering 𝟔𝟖%\mathbf{68\%} of the 4%→30%4\%\to 30\% oracle gap — the contrastive auxiliary doubles as a deployable WHEN trigger at no extra training cost. The one exception is StopCube, whose boundary is purely symbolic: latent-shift collapses to the no-memory baseline (2%2\% vs 12%12\% oracle); on the other 1515 of 1616 tasks, the mechanism is robust to trigger source.

Real-robot sanity check.

On a physical PickXtimes task (“put the blue block into the plate” executed N=3N{=}3 times per episode, six pick-and-place sub-goals; setup in Appendix A.13) with the same π0.5\pi_{0.5}+AP backbone and only the Weaver pathway toggled, Table 1 reports Weaver-off 9/209/20 vs. Weaver-on 𝟏𝟒/𝟐𝟎\mathbf{14/20} — direction consistent with the simulation pattern.

5 Conclusion and limitations

We presented WeaveLA, a cross-subtask latent memory channel that writes a compact 8-token latent at each sub-goal completion event and routes it directly into the next sub-task’s action expert. On a π0.5\pi_{0.5} backbone, gains are mechanism-aligned across three independent stratifications: the lift concentrates on the slice that requires the channel (SwingXtimes N=3N{=}3: 0%→47.8%0\%\to 47.8\%) while N=1N{=}1 stays unchanged, and the contribution is decoupled from simulator boundaries (a model-internal latent-shift trigger recovers 68%68\% of the oracle gap without external supervision). Limitations: latent-shift collapses on count-critical StopCube (2%2\% vs 12%12\% oracle), so symbol-counting tasks still need a learned symbolic detector; characterising the Q-Former instability (Section 4.4) and composing WeaveLA with input-side optimisations such as FrameSamp [8] are left to future work.

A.6 Per-Episode Comparison: Weaver-on vs. Weaver-off

Figure 6 provides a side-by-side rollout comparison of the Weaver module on two timing- and counting-critical RoboMME tasks, with each row showing 99 key-event frames from a single rollout. Every cell preserves both the external camera (left half) and the wrist camera (right half), so the global trajectory and the fine-grained grasp can be inspected together. The SwingXtimes task (top two rows, episode 3) requires the policy to pick up the green cube and shuttle it back and forth between the right-side and left-side targets, completing three full repetitions before pressing the stop button. The StopCube task (bottom two rows, episode 10) requires the policy to watch a cube that automatically oscillates over a target and press the stop button at the exact moment the cube reaches the target for the third time. Rows 11 and 33 are the Weaver-off rollouts of these episodes, and both fail: in SwingXtimes the policy overshoots and performs 3.53.5 swings (an extra half cycle past the third target visit) before pressing the button, so the episode is judged a failure; in StopCube the policy presses the stop button right after the cube passes the target for the second time rather than the third, so the episode is also marked a failure. Rows 22 and 44 are the Weaver-on rollouts of the same episodes: the model correctly completes exactly three swings before pressing in SwingXtimes, and triggers the press at exactly the third target crossing in StopCube so the cube settles directly on the bullseye. Because the initial state and episode index are identical across each pair, the consistent success-with-Weaver / failure-without-Weaver outcome isolates the contribution of the module, indicating that Weaver is essential for sub-task counting and for identifying temporally critical moments in tasks.

The dominant failure mode for π0.5\pi_{0.5}+QF is rollout timeout: 450/800450/800 (56.3%56.3\%) episodes terminated by the per-episode time budget rather than by an incorrect action, compared with negligible timeout rates for π0.5\pi_{0.5}+AP. The Q-Former extractor’s combination of higher inference cost per memory write and a less stable training trajectory leaves the action expert with insufficient time to commit a complete action chunk before the episode times out.

A.9 StopCube what/where/when Ablation Against RoboMME Baselines

StopCube is the canonical count, time-critical task in RoboMME [8]: the policy must press a button at exactly the NN-th moment a moving cube reaches the target, requiring both event counting and precise temporal coordination. The RoboMME paper itself reports that the symbolic upper bound (GroundSG+Oracle, an oracle subgoal planner with the policy still doing low-level control) only reaches 49.7%49.7\% on this task, indicating that precise visuomotor control becomes the primary bottleneck on StopCube. Table 9 compares WeaveLA against the published RoboMME baseline pool as a what/where/when ablation, drawing all baseline numbers from Table 12 of Dai et al. [8]; WeaveLA’s two rows are our π0.5\pi_{0.5}+AP runs.

Where WeaveLA stands.

WeaveLA’s 22.0%22.0\% at the 6-task scale and 12.0%12.0\% at the 16-task scale outperform 12 of the 14 published MME-VLA variants in the baseline pool, both prior-method baselines (MemER, SAM2Act+, both at 0.0%0.0\%), the no-memory π0.5\pi_{0.5} baseline (6.7%6.7\%), and the past-actions variant (4.7%4.7\%). FrameSamp+Modul remains the strongest published number at 42.0%42.0\%. We discuss below (i) why MemER and SAM2Act+ fail at 0.0%0.0\% on this specific task, and (ii) why WeaveLA’s mechanism is orthogonal to FrameSamp+Modul and can be combined with it.

Why MemER fails at StopCube.

MemER [32] couples a VLM that retrieves keyframes from past observations with a symbolic-subgoal policy that executes the retrieved instruction. This is well-matched to dynamic scene-change tasks where the value of memory is recovering an object identity from a previous frame — and indeed the RoboMME paper notes MemER excels on those tasks. StopCube is a different problem: the cube’s position relative to the target evolves continuously between visits, the policy must commit a discrete press action at a specific frame, and there is no past keyframe whose retrieval would tell the policy when to press now. The keyframe-retrieval inductive bias does not produce the temporal precision the task requires. Empirically the model scores 0/500/50.

Why SAM2Act+ fails at StopCube.

SAM2Act+ [10] predicts discrete waypoint actions that are then executed by an external motion planner. The RoboMME paper makes the failure mode explicit: this design “degrades on tasks requiring precise continuous control such as StopCube and InsertPeg.” A waypoint planner cannot represent “press the button at exactly this moment in the cube’s trajectory” — the action space itself is the wrong granularity. Empirically the model also scores 0/500/50.

Why FrameSamp+Modul wins, and why WeaveLA is orthogonal to it.

FrameSamp+Modul reaches 42.0%42.0\% by routing a wide perceptual buffer of past frames into the action expert via AdaLN modulation. Continuous awareness of the cube’s distance from the target across many recent frames is directly useful for time-sensitive control; the RoboMME paper specifically attributes its strength on time-sensitive and motion-centric tasks to this dense perceptual buffer. WeaveLA’s mechanism is structurally different along the when-axis: instead of a dense per-frame buffer, the Weaver writes a single compact 8-token latent at each completed sub-goal event — the natural unit at which the count NN is incremented. Crucially, the two are orthogonal: a dense perceptual buffer answers “how close is the cube to the target right now” while a per-event latent answers “which visit are we currently on”. They occupy different design axes (what is stored and when the write fires) and consume the action expert through compatible interfaces (both are AdaLN/AdaRMS modulation in the same Gemma backbone). In principle, the FrameSamp dense buffer and the WeaveLA per-event latent could be concatenated as parallel modulation streams without any architectural conflict; we leave this combination to future work.

Why WeaveLA already beats other strong baselines.

Among methods that do not use a dense perceptual buffer, WeaveLA is the strongest published number on StopCube. The TokenDrop variants (3.13.1–5.3%5.3\%) drop visual tokens by RGB difference, removing exactly the slow continuous evidence the task needs; the recurrent memory variants (TTT 2.12.1–4.0%4.0\%, RMT 4.74.7–5.8%5.8\%) compress history into a fixed latent state without any explicit alignment to sub-goal events, so the count signal is diluted into the rest of the recurrent state; and the symbolic-subgoal variants with non-oracle subgoal predictors (Gemini, QwenVL) score 0.00.0–3.0%3.0\% because subgoal prediction errors compound across visits. WeaveLA’s sub-goal-event trigger (Section 3.3) avoids these failure modes: the write fires exactly at each visit, and the latent dimensionality is allocated to that single event rather than diffused across a recurrent state.

A.10 Bottleneck Width Ablation: 4 vs. 8 vs. 16 Latents

Table 10 reports per-task success for π0.5\pi_{0.5}+AP on the 16-task training scale across three memory bottleneck widths — N=4N{=}4, N=8N{=}8 (the main configuration), and N=16N{=}16 — all run under the same Stage 2 training schedule. The picture across N∈{4,8,16}N\!\in\!\{4,8,16\} is non-monotonic only in one direction: there is a binding floor below which the bottleneck collapses (N=4N{=}4 aggregates to 2.0%2.0\%, with 0/500/50 on every repetition / dependent-stop task and residual competence only on a handful of memory-of-context tasks), 88 tokens already saturate the channel, and increasing capacity to 1616 tokens does not improve aggregate success (17.5%17.5\% at N=16N{=}16 vs. 23.3%23.3\% at N=8N{=}8). SwingXtimes success is the same at 88 and 1616 tokens (50.0%50.0\%), while every other task either matches or trails the 88-token configuration.

A.11 Staged Training and the weaver_latent_norm Collapse

Training proceeds in three stages, separating action grounding, memory warmup, and full integration; see Section 3.5 for the high-level rationale. Here we provide the diagnostic that motivated the staged design.

We define weaver_latent_norm as the ℓ2\ell_{2} norm of the pooled Weaver latent before semantic normalisation:

weaver_latent_norm=𝔼B​[‖mk−1‖2],\texttt{weaver\_latent\_norm}\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{B}\!\left[\,\bigl\|m_{k-1}\bigr\|_{2}\,\right], (5)

where mk−1m_{k-1} is the output of Eq. 1. While this metric does not directly measure semantic correctness, it reflects whether the raw memory pathway maintains a stable signal for action modulation. In our model the action expert consumes the raw Weaver latent (via AdaRMS), while the alignment and contrastive losses operate on a separately normalised projection. As a consequence, semantic auxiliary losses can remain low even when the raw latent magnitude degenerates, masking a hidden representation collapse.

We compared two training strategies on the 16-task scale: (i) the staged strategy described in Section 3.5, and (ii) a single merged stage that combines all three objectives from the beginning. Both strategies kept action and alignment losses stable. However, in the merged-stage run, weaver_latent_norm decayed monotonically across training and downstream evaluation success collapsed to near zero. In the staged run, weaver_latent_norm remained stable throughout. Figure 7 shows the diagnostic curves.

A.12 Hyperparameters and Compute

π0.5\pi_{0.5}+AP training schedule.

All four π0.5\pi_{0.5}+AP rows (Weaver-on/off ×\times 6-task/16-task) share the same training schedule: Stage 0 task-set adaptation for 40k steps, Stage 1 memory warmup for 8k steps with K=2K{=}2, and Stage 2 full Weaver training for 16k steps with variable K∈{2,3,4}K\in\{2,3,4\}. The model uses an action horizon of 2020 with num_action_steps=8\texttt{num\_action\_steps}{=}8. Trainable parameters include the PaliGemma LoRA adapters (rank 128128, α=128\alpha{=}128 on the gemma_2b_lora variant), the Weaver query latents and projections, and the action-side memory projection that feeds AdaRMS. Optimisation uses AdamW with separate learning rates: base 1×10−51{\times}10^{-5}, LoRA 5×10−55{\times}10^{-5}, memory and modulation 1×10−41{\times}10^{-4}. Stage 2 uses λalign=0.05\lambda_{\text{align}}{=}0.05 and λctr=0.02\lambda_{\text{ctr}}{=}0.02.

Compute.

All training was performed on NVIDIA A100 80GB GPUs with FSDP. The total π0.5\pi_{0.5}+AP training pipeline (Stage 0 + Stage 1 + Stage 2) takes approximately 191191 A100-80GB GPU-hours, broken down as Stage 0 task-set adaptation 36.936.9 GPU-hours, Stage 1 memory warmup 10.510.5 GPU-hours, and Stage 2 full Weaver training 143.6143.6 GPU-hours. The 16-latent bottleneck-width ablation (Appendix A.10) consumes 140.8140.8 GPU-hours on its Stage 2 run under the same schedule. Inference rollouts on the 800-episode RoboMME evaluation suite take approximately 4040 GPU-hours per condition on a single A100. The Q-Former extractor variant trains in approximately the same wall-clock time as π0.5\pi_{0.5}+AP.

Trainable parameter count.

The Weaver module trained on top of π0.5\pi_{0.5} adds approximately 3232M memory-pathway parameters (Weaver query latents, attention-pooling projections, AdaRMS conditioning) and 1414M LoRA-adapter parameters on top of the frozen ∼3.4\sim 3.4B base policy — about 1.4%1.4\% of the base model. Because the memory write is triggered only at sub-goal boundaries rather than every frame, the runtime cost of the memory channel during rollout is negligible compared to dense per-frame memory mechanisms.

A.13 Real-Robot Setup

The real-robot PickXtimes experiment of Section 4.5 runs on a PiPER 6-DoF arm with a parallel-jaw gripper. The workspace is a black-cloth tabletop with a green backdrop holding three coloured cubes (blue, red, green), a white plate, and a target disc. Two cameras feed the policy: a wrist-mounted RGB camera and a third-person RGB camera; an additional Intel RealSense top-down camera is used only for monitoring. At the start of each of the 20 episodes per condition the cubes and plate are reset to randomised positions inside the workspace and the policy is issued the prompt “put the blue block into the plate”; an episode is scored as a success if the blue block is in the plate after N=3N{=}3 pick-and-place repetitions.

A.14 Sub-Goal Boundary Annotation Tool

Sub-goal completion frames for the real-robot demonstrations are produced with a lightweight web-based annotator that synchronises all four camera streams (cam_high, cam_head, cam_left_wrist, cam_right_wrist) and lets the annotator step through frames at adjustable speed and mark / unmark the frame index of each sub-goal completion event. The marked indices are saved per episode (e.g. [30, 54, 88] for a 33-sub-goal episode) and consumed by the Stage 2 training pipeline as the WHEN trigger supervision. Figure 10 shows the annotator interface.
